planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring once frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded border with room for a substantial shrub.

directions: This is a robust, felted-leaf selection of the South African forest spurflower, grown as a substantial soft-wooded shrub rather than a low groundcover. Gray-green, velvety leaves cover upright stems that end in tall, branched spikes of small mauve-purple flowers, produced heavily in autumn and into early winter. It grows quickly and can become leggy, so cut it back hard in early spring to keep a dense, bushy shape and encourage fresh flowering wood. Softwood cuttings root readily through the warm months, making it easy to propagate and share.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or hanging-basket starts after last frost in bright, indirect light or a few hours of morning sun; deep shade dulls the variegation and encourages lanky, less colorful growth.

directions: Grown chiefly for its scalloped, succulent-textured leaves edged in creamy white, this trailing selection releases a sharp, minty-camphor scent when the foliage is brushed or bruised. Slender stems cascade over the rim of a hanging basket or spread as a loose edging along a partly shaded bed, rooting where nodes touch soil. Small lavender flower spikes appear occasionally but are secondary to the foliage display. Pinch stem tips periodically to keep the plant full rather than sparse and trailing.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in lean, fast-draining soil; this species tolerates both open sun and partial shade, making it forgiving of mixed-light borders.

directions: A dense, aromatic South African groundcover with gray-green, succulent-textured leaves that give off a pungent camphor-like odor when crushed, deterring browsing wildlife. Short spikes of small violet-blue flowers appear nearly continuously in warm weather, drawing bees. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most flowering groundcovers, making it useful on slopes or as a low, spreading border. Trailing stems root at the nodes as they spread, so a few starter cuttings quickly fill in a patch.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in humus-rich, moist soil under high shade or dappled woodland light, giving room for an upright multi-stemmed shrub.

directions: Native to forest margins of eastern South Africa, this fast-growing, soft-wooded shrub carries bold, quilted dark green leaves on upright stems. In autumn, when few other shade plants are blooming, it sends up tall spikes densely packed with small violet-purple or white flowers that are a strong draw for bees and sunbirds. Its size and rapid growth make it useful as a seasonal screen or backdrop at the rear of a shaded border. Cut plants back hard after flowering or following any frost dieback to keep growth dense and renew flowering wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring after frost danger has passed, at the front of a partly shaded border or rock garden; unlike most cultivated thunbergias this species does not climb.

directions: This low, many-branched shrublet from the grasslands and open woodland of KwaZulu-Natal breaks from the vining habit shared by most garden thunbergias, staying as a tidy rounded mound instead of climbing. From summer into autumn it carries soft blue to lavender-blue flowers with a pale contrasting throat. Its compact, non-twining form suits the front of a partly shaded bed or a large rock garden where a scrambling vine would be unwelcome. Trim lightly after the main flowering flush to keep the mound neat and encourage rebloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a sturdy pergola, arbor, or into the canopy of a large shrub, in filtered light or partial shade that echoes its native forest-edge habitat; needs consistent warmth and moisture to establish.

directions: A vigorous, woody, twining climber from the tropical rainforests of West Africa, valued for its large, rich violet-blue trumpet flowers held in loose clusters near the stem tips. It performs best scrambling into the dappled light at a forest edge, so a pergola, large arbor, or the canopy of an established shrub in partial shade suits it better than open, exposed sun. Reliable flowering generally requires the sustained warmth of zone 10 and above, with growth slowing noticeably in cooler conditions. Prune after the main flush of bloom to control its size and stimulate new flowering growth.
